1261.title: the Purusha Sukta
1261.hook: sourdough is made with a piece of the last batch. the Purusha Sukta ends with an offering made with an offering, to an offering
1261.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and in Vedic chanting, and its closing line, 'with the offering they offered to the offering', is quoted by teachers reflecting on yajna and dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta drew the sky from a body: the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, the wind from his breath.

A jar on a kitchen counter, with a cloth over the top. Inside, a sour, bubbling paste: a sourdough starter. You make today's bread with a piece of yesterday's. You feed the starter, take some for the loaf, and keep the rest going for next time. Every loaf comes from the one before. Ask where the first starter came from, and the chain runs back further than anyone in the kitchen can see. The Purusha Sukta ends on a loop like that: its last two verses, and the first dharmas.
screen: `A JAR ON THE COUNTER.` → `TODAY'S BREAD FROM YESTERDAY'S.` → `A CHAIN RUNNING BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen gives the measurements of the great offering. Seven sticks were laid around its fire, and three times seven were made its fuel, when the gods, spreading out the offering, bound the Purusha as what was offered. Then verse sixteen, the hymn's last. Yajnena yajnam ayajanta devah. With the offering, the gods offered to the offering. It loops back on itself: the offering is the means, the one who receives, and the act, all at once. Like the starter jar, there's no clean outside place to begin from. The giving comes out of giving. Then: tani dharmani prathamany asan. These were the first dharmas. Dharma is a word this path has met again and again: duty, right order, the way things should go. Here, in a hymn of the Rig Veda, it names the first ways, the first patterns, set down by that offering. The verse ends: those great ones reached the high heaven, where the ancient gods, the Sadhyas, are. So the hymn closes on a loop: the pattern of giving is itself the first dharma. Some readers hear in that something for an ordinary life. What holds a family or a town together may be less a rule laid down from outside, and more a giving that keeps feeding the next giving, like a jar on a counter, kept alive.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing in your life, a skill, a habit, a meal you know how to cook, and ask who gave it to you, then who gave it to them, as far back as you can guess: a grandmother, a teacher, a stranger in a book. Let the chain run back past what you can see, then breathe out and notice you're part of it now; if you pray, you can give thanks for it.
The Purusha Sukta. It ends: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering, and these were the first dharmas.

1262.title: the Gayatri in context
1262.hook: a line on a coffee mug once had a whole speech around it. so does the Gayatri
1262.howItsDone: Hindus who keep the practice recite the Gayatri on its own, at dawn and dusk or with a mala; in Vedic recitation it is also learned as part of Rig Veda 3.62, the hymn it comes from.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta closed on a loop: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering, and these were the first dharmas.
screen: `A GIVING THAT FEEDS THE NEXT GIVING.`

segments.voice: A line printed on a coffee mug. A sentence tattooed on a wrist. A quote pinned above a desk. Each came out of something bigger, a speech, a letter, a chapter, with a speaker and a moment around it. The line works on its own, but put it back where it came from and it says a little more. You met the Gayatri early on this path, heard on its own: at dawn, at a thread ceremony, on a phone before an exam. For six days, it goes back on its string. Today: the hymn it lives in.
screen: `A LINE ON A MUG.` → `IT CAME FROM SOMETHING BIGGER.` → `PUT IT BACK ON ITS STRING.`

segments.voice: The verse sits in the Rig Veda, book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. It begins tat savitur varenyam and ends dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may he stir our thoughts. Now open the hymn around it. Hymn sixty-two isn't a hymn to one god. It moves, in small groups of verses, from one to another. It opens by calling on Indra and Varuna together. Then Brihaspati, the lord of prayer. Then Pushan, the god of roads and safe journeys. Then, partway through, it turns to Savitr, the sun who sets things moving. That turn is the Gayatri: the first verse to Savitr, and the verses after it keep speaking to him a while, asking for his gifts. Then the hymn moves on again, to Soma, and to Mitra and Varuna. So inside its own hymn, the Gayatri is one voice in a chorus, a neighbor among neighbors, standing in the middle, at the moment the hymn faces the sun. Later Hindu practice lifted this one verse out and gave it a life of its own: at the twilight prayers, at the sacred thread ceremony, on strings of beads. That lifting-out is part of its story too. Tradition chose this verse and kept it close. Knowing the neighbors doesn't make it smaller. It shows where it stood when someone first said, this one.
screen: `BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO.` · `A HYMN THAT TURNS FROM GOD TO GOD.` · `THE FIRST VERSE TO SAVITR.` · `LIFTED OUT, KEPT ON ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Hold the last line's meaning, may our thoughts be stirred; if your tradition welcomes you to say the Sanskrit, say dhiyo yo nah prachodayat softly, and if not, the English is enough. Then widen to what's around you: the floor, the walls, the sounds beyond them, the people in the next room or the next street. Let the line sit in the middle of it all, the way the verse sits in its hymn.

1263.title: the Gayatri in context
1263.hook: a laptop clicks shut, a shop pulls down its shutter. a Vedic poet gave that hour a god
1263.howItsDone: Hindus who keep sandhya recite the Gayatri at the day's turning points, dawn and dusk, so the verse to Savitr is said both as the day begins and as it closes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: back in its hymn, one verse among neighbors, the first to Savitr.

Six in the evening. A laptop lid clicks shut. Down the block, a shopkeeper rattles the shutter down. A bus fills with people heading home, and somewhere a pot goes on the stove. Nobody announced it, but the day has turned, and everyone stops at once. A Vedic poet watched this same hour and gave it a god, the god the Gayatri speaks to. Today: who Savitr is in the hymns.
screen: `A LAPTOP CLICKS SHUT.` → `EVERYONE STOPS AT ONCE.` → `THE POET GAVE THE HOUR A GOD.`

segments.voice: The Gayatri asks one thing of Savitr: may he stir our thoughts. To hear that fully, meet him in the other hymns. The Rig Veda pictures him in gold. One hymn calls him hiranyapani, golden-handed, coming on a shining chariot and looking over the creatures of the world. He's the sun, but more than the ball of light: the power that sets things going. A hymn in book two sees him at the other end of the day. When Savitr comes at evening, it says, in paraphrase, the weaver rolls up the cloth she was weaving. The worker sets down a task half done. The traveler turns toward home. The birds go back to their nests. Everything that was moving comes to rest, because Savitr has said so. So he isn't only the god of starting. He's the god of the day's whole swing: he sends people out, and he calls them home. That changes how the Gayatri's request sounds. Asking this god to stir the mind isn't asking for endless motion. It's asking the one who knows when to begin and when to stop. The weaver doesn't finish her row. She rolls up the cloth because the hour has come, and the cloth will be there tomorrow.
screen: `THE GAYATRI SPEAKS TO SAVITR.` · `GOLDEN-HANDED, IN THE HYMNS.` · `AT EVENING, THE WEAVER ROLLS UP HER CLOTH.` · `THE ONE WHO STIRS, AND THE ONE WHO STILLS.`

If you pray, hold the Gayatri's meaning, may our thoughts be stirred, through both halves.

1264.title: the Gayatri in context
1264.hook: the verse everyone calls the Gayatri never says the word gayatri. so where did the name come from?
1264.howItsDone: In Vedic recitation, students learn the meters of the hymns along with their words; the Gayatri is learned both as a verse and as an example of the gayatri meter, and in older texts it is often called the Savitri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context met Savitr: golden-handed, the god who stirs the day awake and, at evening, lets the weaver roll up her cloth.
screen: `THE ONE WHO STIRS, AND THE ONE WHO STILLS.`

segments.voice: A small puzzle. Say the verse through, from tat savitur to prachodayat, and listen for the word gayatri. It isn't there. The verse names Savitr and his radiance, and asks for thoughts to be stirred. It never once names itself. And yet, in everyday speech, it goes by the Gayatri. So where did the name come from? Today: the name, and the other name the verse goes by.
screen: `LISTEN FOR THE WORD GAYATRI.` → `IT ISN'T THERE.` → `SO WHERE DID THE NAME COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Gayatri is the name of a meter, the shape of a verse: how many lines, and how many syllables fill each. Vedic tradition counts the gayatri meter as three lines of eight syllables. You can hear it in the verse: tat savitur varenyam, one line. Bhargo devasya dhimahi, a second. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, a third. Three steps, and done. So the verse is called by the name of the vessel it's poured into, a bit like calling a poem a sonnet, except this verse became so central that its meter's name became its own. The shape isn't rare. The hymn that opens the whole Rig Veda, to Agni, the fire, is set in the same meter, and generations of reciters carried these short verses in their mouths. The verse has a second name, too. Older law books, like the Manusmriti, call it the Savitri: named for the god it speaks to rather than for its shape. Two names, two ways of seeing the same lines. One looks at the form, three short lines easy to carry; the other at who the lines are spoken to. Later tradition went further and honored Gayatri herself as a goddess, the verse become a presence. But under every layer sits a plain fact. Gayatri is a shape, a rhythm a person can hold one breath at a time.
screen: `THE VERSE NEVER SAYS "GAYATRI."` · `GAYATRI: THE NAME OF A METER.` · `THREE SHORT LINES.` · `ALSO CALLED THE SAVITRI.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, count eight slowly in your head, one line of the meter; do it three times for three lines, then rest for a few natural breaths and begin again. If you lose count, start the line over. Nothing is said or chanted, but you're holding the shape the verse is named for.

1265.title: the Gayatri in context
1265.hook: open the Rig Veda to the Gayatri and look for om bhur bhuvah svah. it isn't in the verse
1265.howItsDone: In daily recitation, Hindus who chant the Gayatri may begin with Om and the three vyahritis, bhur bhuvah svah, before the verse itself; traditions vary on further additions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: a verse named for its meter, three short lines, and called the Savitri in older law books.

Open the Rig Veda to book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Run a finger along the line, looking for the words that so often come first when the Gayatri is chanted: Om bhur bhuvah svah. They aren't there. The verse begins tat savitur varenyam. The opening sits outside it, like a doorway built in front of a house. Today: the words before the Gayatri, and why they're said.
screen: `BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO, VERSE TEN.` → `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH: NOT THERE.` → `A DOORWAY IN FRONT OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In daily recitation the Gayatri is often framed. First comes Om, the sacred syllable. Then three short words: bhur, bhuvah, svah. They're called vyahritis, utterances. They aren't part of the Rig Veda verse; they come from the practice of reciting it, and from other Vedic texts that talk about them. One is the Taittiriya Upanishad. In paraphrase: bhur, bhuvah, suvar, these are the three utterances, and a teacher named Mahachamasya made known a fourth, mahas. Then it lays them out like a map. Bhur is this world, the earth. Bhuvah is the space in between. Suvar is the world beyond. And mahas is the sun. So before a person asks the sun to stir their thoughts, they first name where they stand: the ground, the air, the sky. In three words they've walked from the earth under their feet to the heavens, and only then turn to Savitr. Om, then the three worlds, then the verse. Some recitations add more, but that's the core. So when someone says the Gayatri goes Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, they're not wrong about how it's chanted. They're describing the practice, a living tradition of its own. The text and the recitation are both real. They just begin in different places: one at the verse, the other at the doorway in front of it.

segments.voice: Before the sit itself, stand at its threshold for three out-breaths, saying silently here, then between, then beyond, or bhur, bhuvah, svah if you pray. Then step through and rest, letting the breath come and go on its own. When the mind wanders, come back to the doorway, take the three breaths again, and step through once more.

1266.title: the Gayatri in context
1266.hook: earth, sky, heaven: an Upanishad counts the syllables and finds the Gayatri's first line
1266.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Upanishads' readings of the Gayatri as a guide for meditation, contemplating the worlds, the Vedas and the breath while reciting or holding the verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context, and the frame said before the verse: Om, then bhur, bhuvah, svah, earth, the space between, the sky.

A teacher in an old Sanskrit text is playing a counting game. Bhumir, antariksham, dyauh. Earth, sky, heaven. Count the syllables, the text says: eight. The Gayatri's first line has eight too. So whoever knows that first line, it says, wins whatever there is in the three worlds. It sounds like a riddle. It's the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, taking the verse apart line by line. Today: the Gayatri in an Upanishad.
screen: `EARTH, SKY, HEAVEN.` → `COUNT THE SYLLABLES: EIGHT.` → `THE FIRST LINE HAS EIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad gives a whole section to the Gayatri, line by line. The first line is matched by earth, sky and heaven: eight syllables, the three worlds. The second by the three kinds of Vedic verse, the rik, the yajus and the saman: eight syllables, the whole of sacred speech. The third by the three breaths, prana, apana and vyana, the breath in, the breath out and the breath that moves through the body: eight syllables, the whole of life. Worlds, words, breath. Then the text says the Gayatri has a fourth foot. It calls it the visible one, beyond all dust: the sun that blazes. Some readers put it this way: the three lines can be said, and the fourth can only be seen. Then the Upanishad explains the name. In paraphrase: the Gayatri protects the gayas, and the gayas are the breaths; because it protects the breaths, it's called gayatri. That's the Upanishad's own reading of the word, offered as a meditation more than a dictionary entry. It's a big claim made plainly. This one short verse, in the Upanishad's eyes, holds the worlds, the scriptures and the breath of life, and points past itself to a light beyond the dust. The verse we've placed in its hymn and its practice now sits inside the whole of things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context, in the Brihadaranyaka: lines of worlds, words and breath, and a fourth foot, the blazing sun.

Out of all the mountains, which one? Out of all the rivers? In the tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna how to recognize him in the world, and Krishna answers with a long list. Among bodies of water, the ocean. Among trees, the sacred fig. And in the middle, a line about poetry: among meters, I am the Gayatri. Today: the Gayatri in the Gita, and a look back at a week of placing one verse.
screen: `WHICH MOUNTAIN? WHICH RIVER?` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS WITH A LIST.` → `AMONG METERS, THE GAYATRI.`

segments.voice: In the tenth chapter Krishna describes his vibhutis, the ways his glory shows through the world, naming in each kind of thing one where he can be seen. In chapter ten, verse thirty-five, he says: among chants, I am the great Brihat-saman; among meters, the Gayatri; among months, Margashirsha; among seasons, spring. Notice what he names: not exactly the verse to Savitr, but the meter, the three short lines the verse is named for. Some readers hear the famous verse in it too, and the Gita leaves room for that. Either way, a meter of the Vedic hymns is held up as a place where the divine shows. That fits the week, which has been about where the verse shows up. It began with the Purusha Sukta, the hymn of the great Person. In its own hymn, the Gayatri is one verse among neighbors, the first to Savitr, the god who stirs the day and stills it at evening. Its name came from its meter, and older law books call it the Savitri. In recitation it's framed by Om and three words for earth, the space between and the sky. The Brihadaranyaka read its lines as worlds, words and breath, with a fourth foot that blazes. And now the Gita names its meter in Krishna's list. One short verse, seen from six sides. Next, the Rig Veda's other voices: Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna.
screen: `KRISHNA'S LIST OF WHERE HE SHOWS.` · `AMONG METERS, I AM THE GAYATRI.` · `A METER, NOT ONLY A VERSE.` · `ONE VERSE, SEEN FROM SIX SIDES.`

segments.voice: Let the week's pictures come back one at a time, without hurrying: the verse among its neighbors, the weaver rolling up her cloth, three lines of eight counts, the ground, the air and the sky, the breath in, out and through. Give each a breath or two and let it go, and if one stays longer, let it stay. If you pray, end with the Gayatri's meaning: may our thoughts be stirred.
